query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: In near‐equiatomic, multi‐element nanoparticles, the ability to maintain structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) conditions is governed by a temperature‐activated, differential surface segregation process. This process enriches the surface with oxidation‐resistant elements (e.g., Cr or Al) that form a thin, self-healing passivating oxide layer, thereby protecting the internally stabilized high-entropy solid-solution matrix against phase separation and chemical degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized by physical or chemical methods, exhibiting a homogenous compositional distribution and random solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled compositional modification by augmenting (or depleting) the content of an oxidation‐resistant element (such as Cr or Al) while keeping all other synthesis and processing parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Expose the nanoparticles to service‐relevant high-temperature conditions (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) in an environment with reactive (oxidizing) species versus a baseline inert atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a self-healing, passivating oxide layer at the nanoparticle surface, which mediates between the high configurational entropy of the bulk and the temperature-induced surface segregation processes.
generation.mechanism: At processing temperatures, atomic diffusion is activated, leading to preferential segregation of oxidation‐resistant elements toward the nanoparticle surface. Once at the surface, these elements oxidize to form a contiguous, protective oxide layer. This layer impedes further diffusion and mitigates chemical reactions (e.g., uncontrolled oxidation or phase separation) in the bulk, thereby preserving the overall stability of the nanoparticle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with a slightly higher concentration of oxidation‐resistant elements will exhibit the formation of a clearly defined, robust oxide shell that stabilizes the internal solid solution, resulting in reduced phase separation and chemical degradation relative to baseline nanoparticles.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced with strictly near-equiatomic compositions lacking intentional enrichment in oxidation-resistant elements, which may show uncontrolled surface segregation leading to insufficient or patchy oxide layer formation and consequent instability under high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative under moderately oxidizing conditions and within the service temperature ranges stated (773–1173 K for catalytic operation, 473–1923 K for thermoelectric use). Its effectiveness may diminish if the ambient oxidative stress is extreme or if nanoparticle size, defects, or synthesis inconsistencies significantly alter diffusion kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of surface segregation, the quantitative thickness and uniformity of the protective oxide layer, and the interplay with nanoparticle size effects are not fully characterized. Additionally, competing phenomena such as bulk phase separation and sintering might contribute under certain conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles: one set with a controlled moderate enrichment (e.g., an additional 5 at.% of Cr or Al) and a control set with the standard near-equiatomic composition. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature catalytic conditions (773–1173 K) in an oxidizing atmosphere over a fixed duration.
measurements: High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) to image the surface morphology and detect oxide layer formation.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) to determine surface elemental composition and confirm enrichment and oxidation states.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor any bulk phase separation or formation of intermetallic compounds.
Catalytic performance tests to assess stability over time.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enriched nanoparticles do not show a distinct, uniform self-healing oxide layer, or if they display similar levels of phase separation, chemical degradation, and catalytic performance deterioration as the control nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that surface enrichment and subsequent passivating oxide formation govern stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE) [4] . This experiment used Inconel 6

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.
